reason: The sources provide abundant cross-verified data detailing the extreme physics of magnetars and the record-shattering 2004 cosmic blast.
story: In 1979, astronomers detected an unprecedented burst of gamma radiation that saturated spacecraft across the solar system, unveiling an extreme class of dead stars known as magnetars. These city-sized stellar remnants pack more mass than our Sun into a sphere only 12 miles across, wrapped in magnetic fields of 1,000 trillion gauss—the strongest in the known universe. A magnetar is so magnetically fierce that from halfway to the Moon, it could wipe every credit card on Earth, and venturing within 1,000 kilometers would dissolve your cellular chemistry. On December 27, 2004, a starquake on magnetar SGR 1806-20 unleashed a megaflare across 50,000 light-years. In just a tenth of a second, it released more energy than our Sun produces in over 100,000 years. The invisible gamma pulse struck Earth's ionosphere, expanding our upper atmosphere from halfway across the galaxy. Had it erupted within 10 light-years, it would have wiped out our ozone layer.
angle: A magnetar located halfway to the Moon could wipe every credit card on Earth, while a single starquake on one 50,000 light-years away physically expanded Earth's atmosphere.

claims.claim: A magnetar is an ultra-dense neutron star formed by the supernova collapse of a massive star.
Magnetars measure only about 20 kilometers (12 miles) in diameter.
A magnetar's magnetic field can reach an intensity of 1,000 trillion gauss (10^11 tesla).
Magnetars are the most powerful magnetic objects known in the universe.
At a distance halfway between Earth and the Moon, a magnetar could wipe the magnetic stripes of credit cards on Earth.
The first observed giant gamma-ray flare from a magnetar struck the solar system on March 5, 1979.
The March 5, 1979 gamma flare inundated detectors on spacecraft near Venus and orbiting Earth.
Magnetars are powered by the gradual decay of their intense magnetic fields rather than nuclear fusion.
A magnetar's strong magnetic field decays after approximately 10,000 years, ending its active phase.
Tectonic fractures or rearrangements on a magnetar's surface crust are known as starquakes.
The magnetar SGR 1806-20 is located in the constellation Sagittarius on the far side of the Milky Way.
SGR 1806-20 rotates on its axis once every 7.5 seconds.
On December 27, 2004, a massive gamma-ray burst from SGR 1806-20 impacted Earth's atmosphere.
In gamma rays, the December 27, 2004 flare equaled or exceeded the apparent brightness of the full Moon.
In one-tenth of a second, the December 27, 2004 flare released more energy than our Sun emits in 100,000 years.
The 2004 gamma-ray blast struck Earth's ionosphere, ionizing upper atmospheric gas and briefly expanding it.
NASA's newly launched Swift observatory was among the spacecraft that recorded the December 2004 blast.
Radio afterglow emissions from the SGR 1806-20 explosion were tracked by the Very Large Array radio observatory.
A magnetar explosion of that magnitude within 10 light-years of Earth would destroy the ozone layer and trigger a mass extinction.
Magnetars have been detected producing luminous, millisecond-duration fast radio bursts.

disputed: Distance to SGR 1806-20: S2 cites roughly 42,000 light-years (13 kiloparsecs), whereas S1, S3, S5, S6, and S7 cite approximately 50,000 light-years. Scripts should state 'around 40,000 to 50,000 light-years away'.

Energy output comparison: S2 and S3 state the 2004 flare exceeded the Sun's output over 150,000 years, while S5, S6, and S7 state 100,000 years. Scripts should state 'more energy than our Sun produces in 100,000 years'.
Prehistoric extinctions: Speculation that ancient terrestrial extinctions were caused by prehistoric magnetar flares is unconfirmed hypothesis; scripts should describe this as speculative.
